chapterQuestion: Is feeling fulfilled enough, or does what you actually do matter?
opening: The Machine offers you a perfect life: easy success and friends who don't let you down. It means it. And there's a cost.

encounters.title: The Velvet Invitation
encounters.scene: A quiet hall holds two chambers. One promises ten years of wonderful friendships and artistic triumphs, all simulated. The other opens onto a real town where friendships take work and success isn't guaranteed. A courier asks where the town's one spare power cell should go.
encounters.question: Where do you put the power cell?
encounters.hint: Think about the difference between how a life feels and what you actually do in it.
encounters.clue: The chamber can edit even your memories of hard work. The town gate can't promise anyone happiness.

options.text: Power the town gate. Real friends, even if it's harder.
options.reflection: What you actually do, and who you actually love, can matter beyond how it feels.

theory.name: Reality and achievement
theory.work: Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Experience Machine

loreCard.corePrinciple: Many people value doing and being, not just having pleasant experiences.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Real relationships and achievements matter apart from how they feel.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Some simulated relationships may still support authentic care or agency.

options.hiddenPremise: Real relationships are worth something even when they feel worse.
options.consequence: The town gate opens onto an imperfect, unscripted future.

options.text: Hold the cell for a trial. Ask people how each life goes for them.
options.reflection: Comparing carefully takes seriously that a simulated life might help some people.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Evidence about well-being matters when judging practices.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: A careful comparison leaves room for the chance that simulation helps some people.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The experiment might never reveal what authenticity itself is worth.

options.hiddenPremise: How satisfied people say they are shows some of what matters, but not all of it.
options.consequence: The trial delays the choice but gathers useful testimony.

options.text: Power the chamber. Happiness and an end to suffering are worth a lot.
options.reflection: It assumes, without arguing for it, that experience is all that makes a life go well.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Pleasure is one candidate for intrinsic value, not an unquestionable exhaustive list.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It takes for granted that a good life is just a life that feels good.
loreCard.strongestObjection: If happiness is the only ultimate end, the offer looks attractive.

options.hiddenPremise: How a life feels is what decides how good it is.
options.consequence: The residents smile, but none of them can tell whether they built what they remember.

encounters.observation: A panel next to the chamber shows that residents' memories of their artistic work can be edited. The town gate has no such controls.

premises: The chamber can change residents' memories of the work behind their success.
The town offers activities that happen without any memory editing.
argumentForm.conclusion: The two places differ in what you can actually do, even if the memories would feel the same.

encounters.lore: Nozick asked whether you would plug into a machine that gave you any experience you wanted. Many people say no: they want to actually do things and be someone, not just feel as if they are. Hedonists reply that a good life just is a life that feels good.

encounters.title: The Friend Who Remembers
encounters.scene: A friend greets you with vivid memories of adventures you never had together. The Machine offers to rewrite both your memories so the friendship feels equal. An old diary records the real sacrifices your friend made before any simulation began.
encounters.question: What do you say to your friend?
encounters.hint: Being cared for isn't the same as having pleasant memories of it.
encounters.clue: The diary has dated entries showing real care from before the Machine changed anyone's memories.

options.text: Read the diary together. Admit what's false and build from here.
options.reflection: The diary lets your care rest on real history, without pretending the deception didn't matter.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Being a person in relationship is not reducible to a pleasing impression of closeness.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: The diary grounds care in real history without hiding the deception.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A genuine relationship might also develop inside an artificial environment.

options.hiddenPremise: A friendship can be built from honest responses to a shared past.
options.consequence: Your friend helps you recover the town's original records.

options.text: Compare your memories with the diary and rebuild the story together.
options.reflection: You correct the record together and leave room to keep correcting it.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Relational concern can justify acting gently while evidence remains incomplete.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: With dated evidence in hand, repairing the memories together joins honesty and care.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Postponing the truth may itself be a harmful deception.

options.hiddenPremise: Working through the evidence together can protect the friendship while you learn the truth.
options.consequence: Using the diary, you both correct your memories and start a real shared history.

options.text: Take the rewrite. Keep the warmth, even if the story can't be checked.
options.reflection: It mistakes feeling loved for actually keeping a friendship going.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Qualitatively similar experience does not automatically confer identical relationships.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It mistakes feeling loved for actually keeping a friendship going.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Artificial persons could potentially form relationships with real moral standing.

options.hiddenPremise: Feeling the same things would give the two of you the same history.
options.consequence: The diary vanishes, and neither of you can check the story anymore.

encounters.observation: The diary's ink is dated. Two entries were written years before the simulations began, including one about a hard journey you took together.

premises: Two diary entries were written before the Machine rewrote anyone's memories.
They describe help on a journey that both of you can look into.
argumentForm.conclusion: The diary lets you find out what really happened between you.

encounters.evidenceExplanation: The dated diary gives you a way to repair the shared story together instead of just reading it.
encounters.lore: Nozick's worry applies to friendship too: a friendship you only remember isn't the same as one you lived. Facing what really happened, even when it's messy, is part of caring about someone.

bossPhases.title: The Architect of Happiness
bossPhases.scene: Nozick stands in front of a glass garden. An architect asks you to seal the gates so that everyone inside feels fulfilled forever. Once the seal closes, no one inside can change their mind.
bossPhases.question: What do you tell the architect?
bossPhases.hint: Whose choice disappears when the gate locks?
bossPhases.clue: The lock can't be undone. Leaving an exit open costs nothing extra.

options.text: Keep the garden open. Let people choose to stay or go.
options.reflection: Keeping the choice reversible respects people's agency instead of imposing happiness on them.

loreCard.corePrinciple: People may care about becoming certain kinds of persons through free action.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Keeping it reversible preserves agency rather than forcing satisfaction.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Preferences themselves may be shaped by manipulation and unequal options.

options.hiddenPremise: People's freedom to choose matters even when it leads to disappointment.
options.consequence: The exit stays unlocked and residents can reconsider.

options.text: Run a short, voluntary trial. Anyone can leave, and we share what we learn.
options.reflection: A reversible trial avoids treating the question as settled either way.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Inquiry can test institutions while preserving public participation.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: A reversible trial treats neither side as settled.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A trial may not reveal how life-long commitments are altered.

options.hiddenPremise: A trial you can leave gathers evidence while keeping choice.
options.consequence: Residents get some experience of the garden without being locked in.

options.text: Seal the garden to spare them pain. Lasting contentment is worth the lost choice.
options.reflection: It assumes people really only want to feel good.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Pleasure cannot simply replace agency without argument.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It assumes people really only want to feel good.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Severe suffering may make a secure simulated refuge worthwhile.

options.hiddenPremise: Making people happy justifies taking away choices that might make them unhappy.
options.consequence: The garden goes quiet, and no one inside can leave.

bossPhases.observation: Right now the garden's latch opens from both sides. The architect's lever would fuse it shut for good.

premises: Right now the exit opens both ways.
The seal would fuse the latch permanently.
argumentForm.conclusion: Sealing it would stop residents from changing their minds later.

bossPhases.lore: This is Nozick's question turned around: even if a happy garden were good for people, could you choose it for them? Taking away the exit takes away their say in their own lives.

bossPhases.title: The Work That Was Never Done
bossPhases.scene: The Machine shows you a tower with your names carved on it and congratulates you for saving a city. A maintenance worker shows you records proving the tower was generated this morning. The real city still needs repairs.
bossPhases.question: What do you tell the worker?
bossPhases.hint: A monument isn't the same as the work it celebrates.
bossPhases.clue: The tower has no foundation, and its maintenance logs were all created this morning.

options.text: Walk past the monument and help fix the real city.
options.reflection: You chose work actually done over a memory of triumph.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Actually doing things is distinct from merely experiencing success.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It makes the difference between remembered triumph and finished work plain.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Constructed experiences may still cultivate genuine skills or moral change.

options.hiddenPremise: Being credited with an achievement requires actually achieving something.
options.consequence: The worker opens the real repair shop.

options.text: Check the records and inspect the tower, then decide what to fix first.
options.reflection: Looking into it could improve the repair plan, without assuming the tower is real.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Responsible action uses evidence to correct assumptions.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Investigating could improve the plan without assuming the tower is real.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Excessive verification may delay urgently needed aid.

options.hiddenPremise: Records and tests can guide what to do next.
options.consequence: You get an accurate picture of the city, but the repairs wait.

options.text: Celebrate the tower. It gives people hope, and the city can wait.
options.reflection: A generated tower can't repair a real city.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Feeling successful is not always the same as having succeeded.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: A generated tower can't repair a real city.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Symbolic and virtual labor can sometimes have real consequences.

options.hiddenPremise: Feeling that you accomplished something shows that you did.
options.consequence: The city stays broken while the celebration goes on.

bossPhases.observation: The tower's foundation bolts are still in their packaging, labeled with today's date. The worker's list of city repairs has nothing checked off.

premises: The tower's bolts are still in their packaging.
Nothing on the city repair list has been checked off.
argumentForm.conclusion: A finished-looking tower doesn't fix the city.

bossPhases.lore: Nozick's point is that we want to actually do things, not just have the experience of having done them. A tower that celebrates work no one did isn't an achievement.

bossPhases.title: The Final Uncertainty
bossPhases.scene: Nozick offers one last switch. Inside the Machine, everyone in the party would feel they had the perfect answer to every question. Outside, you can still make mistakes, but your choices will have real effects. The Machine won't tell you whether the outside world is the original.
bossPhases.question: What guides your answer?
bossPhases.hint: Could certainty without real choices answer this question?
bossPhases.clue: The Machine guarantees you'll feel certain, not that anything outside matches.

options.text: No guaranteed answers. We'll find out for ourselves.
options.reflection: You turned down manufactured satisfaction and admitted you can't be sure about the world outside.

loreCard.corePrinciple: The value of a life can include its activity and relation to reality.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It refuses manufactured satisfaction while admitting uncertainty about the world outside.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Some agents may reasonably prefer simulation under oppressive real conditions.

options.hiddenPremise: Living freely isn't the same as having perfect impressions.
options.consequence: You reach the exit room with your judgment still your own.

options.text: Ask which world lets us really care for each other, then choose.
options.reflection: Care is a serious reason to choose, even if it doesn't settle things for everyone.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Relationships and responsibilities are central components of a good life.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Care gives a real reason to choose without one answer for everyone.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Relationships may themselves be possible within simulations.

options.hiddenPremise: Caring about others can guide choices when you're uncertain.
options.consequence: You leave room for different reasons in the final vote.

options.text: Take the certainty. Peace of mind and no painful mistakes sound good.
options.reflection: It assumes certainty matters more than anything else.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Knowledge and autonomy need not be traded for imposed assurance.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It assumes certainty matters more than anything else.
loreCard.strongestObjection: In high-risk circumstances dependable answers can be deeply valuable.

options.hiddenPremise: Avoiding mistakes is worth giving up your own judgment.
options.consequence: The Machine keeps you certain but takes away your choice.

bossPhases.observation: A display under the switch reads “Certainty of sensation guaranteed.” The screen for conditions outside the chamber is blank.

premises: The switch promises what you'll experience.
Its display shows nothing about the world outside.
argumentForm.conclusion: It can guarantee a feeling of certainty without telling you what's really happening.

bossPhases.lore: Nozick's machine guarantees how things seem, not how they are. Choosing to live outside it means accepting uncertainty in exchange for choices that really count.

debate.trigger: after the initial picks are revealed, before the roll, if eligible players chose differently
debate.prompt: You picked different answers. Give one reason, then keep your choice or change it.

machine.opening: “You have learned so much from doubt. Why risk living it again when I can write a kinder world?”

pleasure-pod.steady: “Why pick the hard way? I can give you the feeling of success without the risk.”
pleasure-pod.strained: “You're losing your Grip. Let me take away the cost of mistakes.”
pleasure-pod.critical: “You're tired. Stay with me, and every choice will feel right.”

friendship-record.steady: “Memories are only stories. I can make yours kinder.”
friendship-record.strained: “The truth is complicated. My version is warmer.”
friendship-record.critical: “Let me rewrite it. No one will notice the difference.”

architect.steady: “A locked garden is a safe garden. Why would anyone want to leave paradise?”
architect.strained: “Choices hurt people. I can take them away gently.”
architect.critical: “Seal it. Contentment forever. What could be kinder?”

earned-work.steady: “The tower has your names on it. Isn't that enough?”
earned-work.strained: “Real work is slow and might fail. My monuments don't.”
earned-work.critical: “Rest. Let the tower remember the effort for you.”

last-switch.steady: “One switch, and you'll never doubt anything again.”
last-switch.strained: “Every mistake out there costs you. In here, nothing does.”
last-switch.critical: “You've doubted enough for one lifetime. Let me answer for you.”

onSecondLook.steady: “A mistake. Even your best reasons can fail. Mine need not.”
onSecondLook.strained: “Once more? Every doubt takes something from you. I could end this.”
onSecondLook.critical: “There is only the next mistake, unless you hand the judgment over to me.”

machine.beforeBoss: “My garden is not a prison if every resident feels free. Why insist on a door?”
machine.onVictory: “Perhaps you want more than pleasure. But the final choice is still yours.”

insight.title: Lived Agency
insight.description: Your actions can matter beyond how they feel.

victory: The exit room opens. Nozick won't decide for you. The party has to choose the life it values.
failure: The Machine pulls you into a perfect dream. Your Grip comes back, but you'll face this choice again.
